en: A major road with traffic travelling in opposite directions, separated by a central reservation.
The strip or barrier that separates the two directions of traffic on a dual carriageway.
The emergency lane at the side of a motorway, normally for stopping only in an emergency.
A high-speed dual-direction road with controlled access for most traffic, shown by blue signs in the UK.
A temporary traffic system where vehicles travel in the opposite direction to normal, often during roadworks.
Let other traffic go first when they have priority, instead of continuing ahead of them.
The total distance needed to stop: thinking distance plus braking distance.
A place where a road crosses a railway line, often with barriers and warning lights.
A road junction painted with yellow criss-cross lines on the road surface.
A pedestrian crossing controlled by traffic lights, including a flashing amber phase.
A pedestrian crossing with black-and-white stripes where drivers must give way to people waiting to cross.
Bright red lights at the back of a vehicle used only in thick fog to help others see you.
How much air is in each tyre; incorrect pressure affects handling, braking, and tyre wear.
The default UK speed limit when no numbered limit signs are shown (varies by road type and vehicle).
A road without a central reservation separating opposite directions of traffic.
A street where traffic is allowed to travel in only one direction.
When another vehicle has passed you and moved ahead of you.
Marks left on the road when tyres lose grip; on warning signs they often mean a slippery road ahead.
A red-bordered triangle road sign that warns of a hazard ahead.
A larger, busier road that smaller side roads join onto.
Come out onto the road from a side road, driveway, or similar entrance.
A junction where side roads join from left and right at slightly different points, not opposite each other.
A junction where two roads cross, usually forming a plus-sign shape.
The carriageway becomes narrower ahead, so there is less space for vehicles.
Raised ridges across the road that force drivers to slow down (also called sleeping policemen).
A road surface with poor tyre grip, so vehicles can skid more easily.
A road that is bumpy or irregular rather than smooth.
A roadside post or sign showing distance along a route, often in miles.
A route you are required to follow, not just a suggested direction.
A major UK road between towns and cities, usually signed in green with white lettering.
Official road identifiers such as A1 or M25 shown on direction signs.
Small loose stones on a newly surfaced road that can fly up and damage vehicles.
The raised stone or concrete edge between the road and the pavement (US: curb).
A phone you can use without holding it, for example with a speaker or Bluetooth kit.
A sat-nav system that gives turn-by-turn directions while you drive.
Driving the vehicle backwards.
The slight slope built across the road surface, usually higher in the middle.
Passing a slower vehicle by moving alongside and ahead of it.
A major road with traffic travelling in opposite directions, separated by a central reservation.
Low points in the road that can hide traffic until you are close.
A mobile phone that you hold in your hand while using it.
A gearbox that changes gears for you, without a clutch pedal.
Controls that clear mist from the windows so you can see clearly.
The rear-view mirror inside the car, usually at the top of the windscreen.
Turning the vehicle all the way round to go back the way you came.
Looking over your shoulder to see areas the mirrors may miss.
Starting to drive away after you have been stationary.
The brake (often a handbrake) that holds the vehicle still when parked.
A hand signal given by the driver to show other road users what you intend to do.
The upright frames at the edges of the windscreen that can block part of your view.
A street where traffic is allowed to travel in only one direction.
Anything on or near the road that could cause danger or force you to change speed or direction.
Yellow lines painted across the road (from side to side), not along it.
Coming out from a junction or side road onto another road.
The official body that issues and manages driving licences (in Great Britain, the DVLA).
A control that clears mist from the windows so you can see clearly.
Lights above each lane that show whether that lane is open or closed to traffic.
An orange warning light that flashes on a vehicle to make it more noticeable.
Roads where traffic travels in both directions.
The solid white line at a junction that marks where you must stop when required.
The soft or grassy edge beside the road, not meant for normal driving.
A place where a road crosses a railway line, often with barriers and warning lights.
A private path from a house or property that joins the public road.
The side mirrors mounted on the doors, used to see traffic beside and behind you.
Areas around the vehicle that you cannot see in your mirrors alone.
The official body that issues and manages driving licences (Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency).
The plate on a vehicle that shows its registration number.
A large goods vehicle used for carrying cargo (also called a truck).
Driving in a way that uses less fuel, often by smoother acceleration and steadier speed.
Gases and particles released from a vehicle’s exhaust into the air.
A neighbourhood of homes where traffic and pedestrians are often close together.
A ban on stopping your vehicle at all, even briefly (stricter than no parking).
You must not leave the vehicle parked, but brief stopping to drop off may be allowed.
A sign meaning earlier parking or waiting limits no longer apply beyond that point.
Powered road vehicles such as cars, vans, and motorcycles (not bicycles or pedestrians).
A circular junction where traffic usually travels clockwise and you give way to traffic already on it.
A small roundabout, often marked by a white painted circle on the road.
A path or lane intended for bicycles.
An area where cameras check vehicle speeds for enforcement.
Road repairs or construction that may change layout, lanes, or speed limits.
